note: Consolidated teaching view of existing packs plus progression 1. Do not bulk import this as new cards; identities belong to original stable topic/concept/card keys.

topics.title: Control flow
topics.objective: Reason about branches, loops, switch expressions and execution order.

concepts.title: If, else-if and else
concepts.objective: Require boolean conditions, detect unboxing in branches and understand which if owns an else.

cards.explanation: The parenthesized ready expression is the boolean condition. if introduces the statement, the print call belongs to its body, and braces group the body. The condition is checked first; here true permits the body to print start. The syntax is if (condition) followed by a statement or block.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: An if statement tests a boolean condition before its body. Which part of this statement is the condition?

cards.explanation: A false condition skips only the if body, then execution continues at the following statement. finish therefore prints. startfinish assumes the condition is true, start also skips the following unconditional call, and nothing assumes a false if exits the method. An if is optional execution, not a loop or method exit.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: What runs when a simple if condition is false?

cards.explanation: The age comparison is false, so only the else body prints minor. adult chooses the true path, adultminor treats the alternatives as independent statements, and nothing ignores the else. A completed if/else chooses one of its two paths; it does not execute both bodies in sequence.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: An else supplies the alternative when the condition is false. Which message is selected?

cards.explanation: The first comparison fails and the second succeeds, selecting middle. high uses the wrong threshold, middlelow ignores that the final else is skipped after a match, and low ignores the successful middle test. else if is an if nested as the preceding else; write the highest threshold first for these descending score bands.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: An else-if chain tests later conditions only after earlier conditions fail. Which band applies?

distractors: Compilation fails: if permits only one statement.
cards.explanation: Both calls are inside one block and run in order because paid is true. receipt and ship each omit one statement. An if accepts a block as its body, so the multiple statements are legal. Group related conditional actions with braces so their shared condition is visible.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: Braces make several statements one branch body. Which actions happen here?

distractors: Compilation fails: overlapping conditions are forbidden.
cards.explanation: An else-if chain chooses its first matching branch. The >=60 condition succeeds, so the >=90 test is never reached. Java does not select the most specific or largest threshold automatically, and overlapping conditions are legal. fail ignores the successful first test. To award distinction here, test >=90 before >=60.
cards.coverage_gap: Overlapping else-if thresholds depend on branch order.

distractors: Compilation fails: both conditions can be true.
cards.explanation: Separate if statements are evaluated independently. Both conditions hold at zero stock, so both messages print in source order. Printing only low treats the second statement as an else-if, while empty alone skips a true earlier branch. Java permits overlapping conditions; use else-if when only one notification should be selected.
cards.coverage_gap: Independent if statements differ from exclusive else-if chains.

distractors: Compilation fails: the else has no matching if.
cards.explanation: The braces make the entire inner block the outer if body, so else belongs to loggedIn. loggedIn is true and admin is false; neither message is printed before done. guestdone binds else to the inner if despite the closing brace, admindone ignores admin=false, and the outer if is a valid match for else.
cards.coverage_gap: Explicit blocks alter branch grouping relative to dangling-else starter.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: the assignment expression has type int.
distractors: It prints yes because assigning 1 makes the condition truthy.
It prints no because assignment expressions are always false.
It compiles but throws because assignments are forbidden at runtime.
cards.explanation: Java if conditions require boolean or Boolean. Assigning 1 to an int produces an int, not a truth value; this is not the score == 1 comparison.
Without braces, the else belongs to the nearest eligible if: if (inner). outer is true, inner is false, so its else prints B; indentation does not change binding.

The else statement is reached only when cached is false. Because the first branch runs, even the later condition is skipped and lookups stays zero. cache 1 evaluates a skipped test, cache lookup 1 wrongly runs both alternatives, and lookup 1 ignores the true first condition. Side effects in branch tests follow control flow.
cards.coverage_gap: A successful branch suppresses later else-if condition side effects.

distractors: Compilation fails: a method cannot contain two return statements.
cards.explanation: The guard returns guest before the dereferencing call is reached. Return exits that method invocation immediately, so a missing name does not reach toUpperCase. Printing null assumes the argument is returned unchanged; NullPointerException ignores the guard; multiple return statements on different paths are legal. Locale.ROOT makes the non-null path independent of default locale.
cards.coverage_gap: Early-return null guard prevents later dereference.

distractors: Compilation fails: return prevents any following statement from being reachable.
cards.explanation: The invalid branch returns before calls++ for this invocation. Other inputs can take the false branch and reach the work, so the statements after the conditional are reachable. invalid 1 performs work after a returned invocation, saved 1 ignores the validation, and the compile-error option confuses conditional return with unconditional return.
cards.coverage_gap: Guard clauses suppress downstream work while leaving valid paths reachable.

distractors: Compilation fails: equals returns Boolean rather than boolean.
cards.explanation: Boolean.TRUE is non-null; its equals method returns primitive false for a null argument. The else prints off without unboxing enabled. on incorrectly treats missing as true, the exception option assumes if directly tests enabled, and equals returns a primitive boolean accepted by if. This explicitly implements null-as-disabled semantics.
cards.coverage_gap: Null-safe Boolean decision instead of directly unboxing a nullable condition.

cards.explanation: The first reference-null check handles the missing value before the later unboxing condition can be reached. It preserves a separate unset outcome rather than mapping null to false. no and yes ignore the first branch, and NullPointerException would require evaluating approved as a condition, which this input does not do. Distinguish missing from disabled when the domain needs three states.
cards.coverage_gap: Explicit first null branch preserves a third state instead of conflating missing with false.

distractors: Compilation fails: && cannot combine a reference check and a method result.
cards.explanation: The left comparison is false, so && skips isEmpty. Both operands have boolean type, and the branch selects missing. The exception option overlooks short-circuiting, text overlooks the failed guard, and mixing two kinds of boolean-producing expressions is legal. Reversing their order would dereference null before checking it.
cards.coverage_gap: Practical guard order prevents nullable text dereference.

distractors: Compilation fails: && and || cannot appear in the same expression.
cards.explanation: && binds more tightly than ||, so first groups as (loggedIn && owns) || admin and accepts the admin flag independently of login. second requires loggedIn before either ownership/admin can permit access. false/false overlooks the independent admin alternative; true/true ignores the explicit outer login requirement; mixed operators are legal. Choose parentheses to express the intended policy.
cards.coverage_gap: Permission predicates expose precedence versus explicitly grouped login requirement.

distractors: It prints no because null means false.
It prints yes because the reference exists.
It fails because Boolean is not a condition type.
cards.explanation: Boolean is allowed as a condition but must be unboxed. A null reference throws before either branch runs; null does not act as a false primitive boolean.

distractors: Compilation fails: text cannot be used in the && operand.
cards.explanation: A successful positive pattern match introduces text for the && right operand and the true if body. The payload is a two-character String, so GO prints using Locale.ROOT. The scope-error option ignores flow-sensitive binding, other ignores the true predicate, and safe type testing/binding does not cause a cast failure.
cards.coverage_gap: Successful instanceof pattern binding is available to an AND predicate and true body.

concepts.title: For and enhanced-for loops
concepts.objective: Count iterations accurately and distinguish a loop body from a trailing empty statement.

cards.correct_option: Initialize step once; test before each body; increment after each body.
distractors: Initialize step before every body; test after each body; increment first.
Test once; initialize after testing; increment before the body.
All three header parts run only once.
cards.explanation: The initializer creates step as zero once. The test admits bodies at zero and one; the update increments after each normal body; the final test at two fails. This prints 01. Reinitializing each visit would erase progress, testing only once would not bound iteration, and executing every clause once ignores repeated testing and updates.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: Which description correctly identifies the three header parts?

cards.explanation: Initialization gives two, each successful test permits the current value to be appended, and the update moves to the next value. The inclusive test includes four. 23 treats <= as <, 345 updates before the first body, and 222 assumes the initializer reruns. This builds a trace rather than relying on a memorized iteration count.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: The loop variable can be used in the body. What values are visited?

cards.explanation: Bodies run for count zero, one and two, printing one mark each. Two marks drops a valid visit, four includes the failing test at three, and 012 confuses the counter with the body output. The condition controls whether the body runs; the body determines what gets printed.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: A counter can control repetition even when its value is not printed. How many marks appear?

cards.explanation: The colon separates the iteration-variable declaration from the array being traversed. price receives three then seven, and the body accumulates ten. Three stops after the first element, seven replaces rather than accumulates total, and two counts elements instead of their values. Mutation and hidden-conversion details come after understanding this ordinary traversal.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: The enhanced-for form reads successive elements without an explicit index. What does this traversal produce?

cards.explanation: The body runs for i = 0, 1 and 2. The exclusive upper bound excludes 3, and the sum is 3; counting iterations is not the same as summing the index.
The inclusive bound includes i = 3, so the body adds 1 + 2 + 3. Omitting the final iteration or including 4 gives the incorrect alternatives.

The loop visits indices 2, 1 and 0, printing 9, 7 and 4. >=0 includes the first element; using >0 would omit it. Forward output reverses the specified direction, and length-1 is a valid initial index. On an empty array it starts at -1 and performs no access.
cards.coverage_gap: Reverse traversal includes index zero and starts at length minus one.

cards.explanation: Starting at zero with step two visits indices 0, 2 and 4. The next index is 6, but the condition fails before accessing it. Omitting nine incorrectly rounds the iteration count down, 6/8 starts at index one, and the exception option treats an invalid future index as an executed access.
cards.coverage_gap: Non-unit stride with an odd-sized input and a pre-access bound test.

cards.explanation: Each iteration advances left and decreases right; the condition is retested after both updates. The pairs are 0:3 and 1:2, then 2<1 is false. Visiting 2:1 ignores termination, fixed right values omit its update, and one pair stops too early. The condition expresses crossing rather than an array length boundary.
cards.coverage_gap: Multiple indices update together and stop when an inward scan crosses.

distractors: Compilation fails: update expressions cannot depend on each other.
cards.explanation: The for update expressions execute left to right. i++ runs before mirror=i, so the second body sees both as one. 1:0 reverses that update order, 0:1 assumes updates precede the first body, and dependencies between updates are legal. This matters when several loop-state variables are maintained in one header.
cards.coverage_gap: Dependent update expressions run left to right after the body.

distractors: Compilation fails: a for loop requires a condition.
cards.explanation: An omitted for condition permits repeated execution until an explicit transfer exits it. The pre-increment reaches three before printing, so break skips that print and exits. 123 prints after the terminating guard, 012 treats pre-increment as post-increment, and Java permits the empty condition. This is a termination design example, not a claim that every unbounded loop is safe.
cards.coverage_gap: Omitted for condition can be safely bounded by an explicit guard/break.

cards.explanation: The semicolon is the entire empty loop body. The loop still increments i until its condition fails at 3; the following print is executed once outside the loop.

distractors: Compilation fails: an empty array initializer is invalid.
cards.explanation: length is zero, so i<=length admits i=0, but an empty array has no valid indices. The access throws before printing. Zero is not a valid default element, empty initializers are legal, and the normally-empty traversal requires i<length. This boundary bug occurs even before considering nonempty inputs.
cards.coverage_gap: Inclusive traversal bound fails on empty input rather than skipping the body.

distractors: Compilation fails: enhanced-for variables cannot be assigned.
cards.explanation: Each iteration variable receives the current element value. Assigning or incrementing that primitive local does not write back to the array slot. The variable need not be final, so assignment is legal; 11/12 wrongly assumes write-through, and 10/10 additionally replaces rather than adds. Use indexed assignment to update primitive array elements.
cards.coverage_gap: Enhanced-for primitive iteration variable is a value copy, not a writable array element alias.

distractors: Compilation fails: enhanced-for cannot mutate objects.
cards.explanation: The iteration variable copies each reference, so it still refers to the same object as the corresponding slot. Field mutations are therefore visible through the array. 1/2 confuses copying a reference with cloning its object, 10/10 ignores +=, and no language rule forbids object mutation merely because enhanced-for is used.
cards.coverage_gap: Reference-valued enhanced-for permits mutation of the referenced elements.

distractors: Compilation fails: assigning the iteration reference is forbidden.
cards.explanation: Reassigning the iteration local changes that local reference, not the array slot that supplied it. The original element therefore stays at one. Nine assumes a write-back reference binding, zero invents a reset, and non-final iteration locals may be assigned. This deliberately contrasts with mutating a field on the referenced element.
cards.coverage_gap: Reassigning enhanced-for reference does not replace its source array slot.

cards.explanation: For array iteration, the enhanced-for expression is evaluated once and its array is retained for traversal. Both elements contribute six and the provider is called once. Two calls would reevaluate for each element, three would add a terminating reevaluation, and two as the sum omits the second element. Expensive or stateful providers do not rerun merely because the body repeats.
cards.coverage_gap: Enhanced-for array expression is evaluated once rather than per iteration/test.

distractors: Compilation fails: enhanced-for never permits unboxing.
cards.explanation: Each Integer element is converted to int for the iteration variable. The first value is added; the null element then fails unboxing before its body runs, so the final print is not reached. Null is not skipped or converted to zero, and this implicit unboxing conversion is legal at compile time. Use reference iteration plus an explicit null policy when needed.
cards.coverage_gap: Enhanced-for variable conversion can implicitly unbox a nullable element.

concepts.title: While and do-while loops
concepts.objective: Distinguish pre-tested/post-tested loops and include side effects from the final failed test.

cards.explanation: Each body prints the current positive value and decreases it. At zero the pre-body test fails, so 321 prints. 32 stops too soon, 3210 includes a value excluded by the test, and 333 ignores the state update. Identify both the condition and the progress step to explain termination.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: A while loop repeats while its condition stays true. What sequence is produced?

cards.explanation: The first test is true, the body runs once, and the next test reads the changed false value. Zero ignores the initial true value, two grants a body after a failed test, and nontermination assumes the original value was cached. while reevaluates its condition before every possible body visit.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: Does while keep using only its original condition value?

cards.correct_option: The body increments value before the first condition test.
distractors: The condition is tested before the body.
The trailing semicolon creates a second loop.
The body runs once and never repeats.
cards.explanation: do places the body before the condition, and the trailing semicolon is part of this statement syntax. The first increment produces one, the true test repeats the body, and the next increment/test ends at two. The first alternative describes while, a second loop is not introduced, and do can repeat beyond its mandatory first body.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: In this do-while form, which step happens first?

distractors: while performs none, do performs one: prints 0 1.
while includes one extra body: prints 3 2.
cards.explanation: The initial while test succeeds, so both forms increment twice until their counters reach two. The pre-test/post-test distinction matters when the initial condition is false, not on every input. 0/1 applies that different initial case here, 2/1 suppresses a true do test, and 3/2 adds a while body after its false test.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: Both loops have progress. Why are their final values equal for this input?

cards.explanation: while checks the condition before the body. count < 0 is initially false, so the increment never runs; a loop does not guarantee one iteration.
do-while executes its body before checking the condition. The increment runs once, then 1 < 0 is false; it differs from the corresponding while loop.

distractors: Compilation fails: every false-valued loop condition makes its body unreachable.
cards.explanation: run is an ordinary local, not a constant expression. The body is reachable under the language rules even though the actual first test is false, so the source compiles and skips it. The compiler-error option confuses this with while(false); bodydone ignores the runtime value; infinite execution invents a true condition.
cards.coverage_gap: Ordinary false-valued loop local differs from constant-false reachability rules.

cards.explanation: A do-loop continue still evaluates the condition. Each of the first two bodies increments attempts and continues; the second condition test ends the loop. No work text appears. Skipping the condition would give the wrong counts, reaching work assumes a third iteration that never occurs, and one iteration ignores the true first test.
cards.coverage_gap: Continue in do-while transfers to its condition, including condition effects.

cards.explanation: continue skips index++, so every admitted body sees the same zero at index zero. The external budget eventually fails on its fourth test, yielding 0/4. Advancing past zero or traversing both values assumes progress that was skipped; index never becomes invalid. Move progress before the skip or make it unavoidable to prevent nontermination without the diagnostic budget.
cards.coverage_gap: While continue can bypass essential progress; bounded diagnostic safely exposes the repeated state.

cards.explanation: Only the two values before the zero sentinel are added. index advances in the body, so it remains two when the condition sees zero. 15/4 ignores the sentinel, 6/3 consumes it despite the failed test, and checking the bound first with && also prevents an out-of-range access if no sentinel exists.
cards.coverage_gap: Sentinel scanning combines boundary protection and stopping without consuming sentinel.

cards.explanation: The first two readiness tests fail and each executes the body. The third succeeds, so !ready is false and no third body increment occurs. attempts counts failed bodies, while calls counts tests, including the final successful test. 3/3 conflates those counts, 5/5 ignores early success, and 2/2 omits the terminating test.
cards.coverage_gap: Retry body count differs from service test count at early success.

cards.explanation: The comparison uses the old value and then increments i. Tests with old values 0 and 1 pass; the final test with old value 2 fails but still increments i to 3.

distractors: Compilation fails: assignments inside loops never establish definite assignment.
cards.explanation: A do loop executes its body before testing the condition. The assignment therefore happens before any normal exit; with no arguments the first test ends the loop and seven prints. Loop assignments can establish definite assignment when every exiting path supplies it; zero invents a local default, and the shown condition is false on its first test.
cards.coverage_gap: Guaranteed do-loop body can establish assignment before a later local read.

concepts.title: Break and continue
concepts.objective: Distinguish exiting a loop from skipping its current body and understand for updates after continue.

cards.explanation: The first body prints found, then break exits the loop and the following print runs. found alone treats break as a method return, done skips the admitted body, and nontermination ignores break. A true loop condition does not imply an infinite run when a reachable break supplies an exit.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: A break exits its containing loop immediately. Which code remains reachable at runtime?

cards.explanation: The body appends at values one and three, while continue skips the append at two. The for update still executes after that continue. xxx ignores the skip, x treats continue as break, and an endless loop incorrectly skips the for update. This introduces skip versus exit before nested target cases.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: A continue skips the rest of the current iteration. Which markers are suppressed?

cards.explanation: break ends the first scan at two, leaving only its first visit counted. continue skips counting two but permits three, so the second count is two. 2/2 gives break a skip-only meaning, 1/1 turns continue into exit, and 2/1 reverses the rules. Choose break when no later elements should be considered, continue when only the current one is unsuitable.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: Two scans meet the same marker. How do exit and skip differ?

cards.explanation: break exits the loop when i is 3, before that value is added. Only 1 and 2 contribute; it does not merely skip the third iteration.
continue skips only the rest of the current iteration. The loop still visits 3 and 4, adding 1 + 3 + 4; it neither adds 2 nor exits the loop.
A continue targeting a basic for loop proceeds to its update expressions. i advances past 1, so the loop terminates at 3 and visits is incremented for 0 and 2 only.

The i=0 body completes and runs both update expressions once. The i=1 body breaks, so neither update runs again. 2/2 updates after break, 1/2 runs only one of the updates without justification, and 3/3 ignores termination. This contrasts with continue, which proceeds to a for-loop update.
cards.coverage_gap: Break suppresses the for update rather than merely skipping the body tail.

distractors: Compilation fails: break cannot exit a do loop.
cards.explanation: break completes the loop abruptly and skips its condition, so tests remains zero. body 1 incorrectly evaluates the trailing test, repeated bodies ignore break, and do loops are valid break targets. Unlike the do-continue example, this transfer exits rather than returning to the test.
cards.coverage_gap: Do-loop break skips the trailing test; intentional contrast to continue.

cards.explanation: break targets the nearest enclosing switch here, not the loop. The first iteration prints A then X, and the second prints B then X. A exits too far, ABX omits the first post-switch step, and AXB omits the second. A loop-targeting labeled break would be needed to exit that outer loop directly.
cards.coverage_gap: Unlabeled switch break does not exit its containing loop.

distractors: Compilation fails: continue is forbidden inside a switch.
cards.explanation: A switch is not a continue target; the enclosing loop is. At i=1 the rest of that loop body is skipped, including X, and the for update still runs. Printing one ignores continue, the extra X treats continue like switch break, and the nested continue is legal because a loop encloses it.
cards.coverage_gap: Continue inside switch targets the enclosing loop rather than the switch.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: an unlabeled break needs an enclosing loop or switch.
cards.explanation: An if statement is not a target for an unlabeled break. The source is rejected because there is no enclosing loop or switch to exit. The condition being true does not turn break into return, ignore it or defer the problem to a runtime exception. Use an appropriate control structure or method return for an early exit.
cards.coverage_gap: Unlabeled break cannot target an if statement or the surrounding method.

verification.code:
if (args.length == 0) break;
System.out.print("done");

cards.explanation: continue outer targets the while condition, bypassing the inner for updates entirely. Two admitted outer bodies each leave on their first inner visit; the final failed outer test makes tests three. Counts with updates incorrectly execute the inner loop continuation, and two tests omits the final false evaluation. The target loop determines where control resumes.
cards.coverage_gap: Outer while continue bypasses inner for update and includes the final outer test effect.

concepts.title: Nested loops and labels
concepts.objective: Identify the loop targeted by unlabeled/labeled break and continue without skipping or inventing iterations.

cards.explanation: For each of two rows, a freshly initialized inner loop performs three visits: six total. Five adds loop lengths rather than composing repetitions, three counts one row, and two counts outer visits rather than inner bodies. Learn the unmodified nested traversal before tracing breaks or labels that interrupt it.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: Nested loops complete inner visits for each outer visit. How many body visits occur?

cards.correct_option: It names the block; ordinary execution still prints AB.
distractors: It repeats the block: prints AAB.
It skips the block: prints B.
It creates a variable named phase.
cards.explanation: A label names the immediately following statement as a possible transfer target. By itself it neither repeats nor skips execution, so the block then the following print produce AB. Labels are not variables and do not create stored values. Labeled break/continue examples build on this basic meaning.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: What does the label before this block do when no transfer refers to it?

cards.explanation: The unlabeled break targets the inner loop. Each of the three outer iterations increments visits at j = 0, then breaks at j = 1; the outer loop continues.
break outer exits the labeled outer loop immediately after the first increment. An unlabeled break would exit only the inner loop and allow later outer iterations.
continue outer ends the current outer iteration when j = 1 and executes the outer for update. Each outer iteration therefore increments visits only at j = 0.

distractors: Compilation fails: a break label must name a loop.
cards.explanation: A labeled break may exit an enclosing labeled statement, including a block. With no arguments it skips B and resumes after the block, printing C. ABC ignores the transfer, A treats it as a method return, and break does not require a loop label. Continue has the stricter loop-target requirement.
cards.coverage_gap: Labeled break can exit an ordinary block rather than only a loop.

distractors: Compilation fails: a label cannot target the nearest loop.
cards.explanation: continue inner selects the inner for update and next test. Its two iterations run for each of two rows, giving four body visits and four updates. 2/2 jumps to the outer loop instead, 4/0 skips required for updates, and labels can explicitly identify the nearest enclosing loop. Labels do not inherently mean an outer-loop transfer.
cards.coverage_gap: A labeled inner continue preserves that loop update and does not skip outer iterations.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: continue must target a labeled loop, not a block.
cards.explanation: A continue target must be an enclosing while, do or for statement. retry labels a block, so the code is rejected. It cannot jump to the block start, silently skip it or fall through and print work. A labeled break could exit the block, but a continue cannot turn it into a loop.
cards.coverage_gap: Continue label target must be a loop even though break permits blocks.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: finished does not label an enclosing statement at the break.
cards.explanation: A labeled break must refer to a label on a statement that encloses the break. The finished block has ended before the loop, so its label is unavailable as a transfer target. Compilation prevents any output; Java labels are not arbitrary goto destinations and cannot re-enter a completed block or create repetition.
cards.coverage_gap: Label availability depends on enclosing statement, not prior declaration order.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: the nested label outer conflicts with an enclosing label.
distractors: Throws IllegalStateException because the break target is ambiguous.
cards.explanation: A label cannot redeclare the name of an enclosing labeled statement. The compiler prevents the conflict instead of resolving it to the nearest label at runtime. There is no normal execution, infinite run or dynamic ambiguous-target exception. Different names make intended transfer targets explicit; label namespaces still have enclosing-scope restrictions.
cards.coverage_gap: An enclosing label name cannot be reused on a nested labeled statement.

concepts.title: Switch statements and case labels
concepts.objective: Trace colon-style case groups, missing matches and null selectors.

cards.explanation: The selector value two matches case 2, so execution starts there and break exits the switch. save starts at the wrong label, saveopen assumes all labels run from the top, and unknown ignores the match. Labels select an entry point; they are not independent if conditions evaluated as separate bodies.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: A switch selector chooses a matching case label. Which command runs?

cards.explanation: No case constant equals nine, so default supplies the fallback body. Nothing overlooks default, concatenating all bodies ignores entry selection and the breaks, and no language rule creates IllegalArgumentException for an unmatched constant here. An absent default would give different behavior for a traditional statement.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: What is the ordinary role of default when no constant case matches?

cards.explanation: break exits this switch, then Z prints. A alone treats break as return from main, ADZ ignores break and falls through, and Z skips the matched case. This establishes the basic target before a switch is nested in a loop, where choosing the correct containing target becomes harder.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: After a matched case breaks, does ordinary execution continue?

distractors: Compilation fails: every rule needs break.
Compilation fails: every arrow switch must return a value.
cards.explanation: The matching arrow rule executes its print call and completes the statement without entering later rules. No break is required for arrow-rule fall-through prevention, and a switch statement need not produce a value. The concatenated option applies colon fall-through behavior to arrows. This is a statement because its selected call is executed for its effect.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: Arrow rules select a body without colon-style fall-through. What runs?

distractors: Compilation fails: String selectors must be literals.
cards.explanation: String constant cases match using String content equality, not object identity. The new String contains go and therefore selects run. other applies ==-style identity reasoning, the compiler-error choice invents a literal-only selector restriction, and both selector and label are String, so no cast failure is involved.
cards.coverage_gap: String switch matching uses contents even for a non-interned selector.

distractors: Compilation fails: each case label needs its own body.
cards.explanation: A statement group may have multiple labels. Either one or two enters the same body once, and break exits. smallsmall treats matching multiple labels as duplicated execution, other ignores the matching label, and labels need not each have independent statements. This is intentional sharing rather than missing-break fall-through between populated groups.
cards.coverage_gap: Multiple colon labels can intentionally share one body.

cards.explanation: This ordinary int switch statement may omit default. With no matching case, none of its body runs and execution continues after the switch. Switch expressions have different exhaustiveness requirements.
Execution begins at matching case 2 and falls through into case 3. Its break prevents default from running; earlier case 1 is not revisited.

With no matching case, execution starts at default, wherever it appears. It then falls through to the later case group until break. D assumes default implicitly stops, ADB incorrectly executes earlier groups, and B skips the default body. Source placement changes fall-through, not matching priority.
cards.coverage_gap: Middle default location determines forward fall-through for an unmatched selector.

distractors: Compilation fails: default must precede no cases.

DBX incorrectly starts at default, DX ignores the matching constant, and this traditional constant-only layout is legal despite default being first. This contrasts with the earlier unmatched-selector middle-default example.

cards.explanation: The selector expression is evaluated once and post-increment yields one, so case one is selected. Its assignment stores three without re-running matching, and break exits. three 3 uses the later value to choose the initial case, one three 3 rematches after mutation, and other 2 ignores the yielded selector and explicit assignment.

distractors: Compilation fails: boxed integral selectors are forbidden.
cards.explanation: Byte is a supported boxed selector type for this constant switch. Its non-null value is unboxed and compared with the compatible constant two. The wrapper does not require identity matching against a case object, the syntax is legal, and no cast to a different wrapper occurs. A null Byte would instead fail unboxing.

distractors: It prints other via the default case.
It prints go after converting null to text.
It fails because String selectors are unsupported.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: expected is not a constant expression usable as this case label.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: the two case constants both equal 2.

Java does not choose the first, choose the later one, or treat the textually different expressions as two runnable cases. Replace the duplicate with a distinct value or share one label/body.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: 128 cannot be converted to the byte selector type for this label.
cards.explanation: The constant case label must be compatible with the selector type. The int constant 128 does not fit byte, so it cannot use the representable-constant narrowing allowed here. Compilation fails even though the shown selector is one and would never equal 128. Java does not silently ignore or wrap the label, nor check it by a runtime exception.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: direct entry to case 2 can read value before assignment.

cards.explanation: Colon groups share the enclosing block scope, so value is visible in the later group. Definite assignment is different: matching case two enters after its initializer, making the read invalid. Seven assumes execution fell through case one, zero assumes a local default, and the scope-error option confuses visibility with assignment safety.
cards.coverage_gap: A visible colon-case local may be unassigned when matching enters a later group directly.

concepts.title: Switch expressions and yield
concepts.objective: Predict non-falling-through arrow rules and return values from exhaustive switch expressions.

distractors: Both alternatives are combined: prints readyother.
Compilation fails: switch cannot initialize a variable.
cards.explanation: This switch is used as the initializer for label. Case one selects ready, which is stored and printed. The selector is not replaced by the result, alternatives are selected rather than concatenated, and switch expressions are legal initializers. The semicolon ends the surrounding variable declaration.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: A switch expression produces a result. Where is the selected value stored?

distractors: Compilation fails: yield is only for loops.
cards.explanation: The selected rule computes base and yield supplies six as the switch-expression value. Four ignores the added two, zero chooses the unselected default, and yield is specifically a result transfer for an enclosing switch expression rather than a loop construct. A rule block needs a result-producing or permitted abrupt path.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: A multi-statement rule can compute a value and yield it. What is the result?

cards.correct_option: default covers the unmatched value: prints 20.
distractors: Java invents a zero result: prints 0.
The first case is used as a fallback: prints 10.
Compilation fails: every int must have its own case.
cards.explanation: default handles every otherwise unmatched non-null int value, selecting twenty here and making this expression exhaustive. There is no invented zero or first-case fallback. Listing each possible int separately is unnecessary when default covers the remainder. Exhaustiveness and advanced reference/null rules build on this ordinary result guarantee.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: Why does this expression supply a value for code 7?

cards.explanation: An arrow rule supplies its value without falling through into later rules. The matching rule yields two; no break statement is necessary.

distractors: Compilation fails: arrow rules cannot have multiple case constants.
cards.explanation: A comma-separated list of constants labels one arrow rule. Matching three evaluates its expression once and yields small. It does not execute once for every constant, skip the matching rule, or require separate arrows. Grouping provides shared behavior without colon-style fall-through.
cards.coverage_gap: Grouped arrow constants select one result once.

cards.explanation: yield supplies the value of the enclosing switch expression. The local value is 20 and the yielded expression is value * 2; yield is not a method return.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: the switch expression is not exhaustive.
distractors: It prints 10 because selector currently contains 1.
It prints 0 because unmatched values receive an implicit default.
It throws only if selector contains a value other than 1.
cards.explanation: A switch expression must cover all possible selector values. A non-final int variable initialized to 1 does not limit its static domain; add a default rule for this int expression.

verification.expected: does not cover all possible input values

distractors: Compilation fails: all switch expressions require a default label.
cards.explanation: Listing every constant of this enum establishes exhaustiveness without default. CLOSED selects zero. One selects the wrong constant, a mandatory-default rule is too strong, and state is not null. This checks source-level coverage for the shown enum; separately compiled changes to enum definitions require additional compatibility reasoning.
cards.coverage_gap: Complete enum constant coverage can make an expression exhaustive without default.

distractors: Compilation fails: every switch rule must yield a value.
cards.explanation: A switch-expression rule may throw rather than produce a value. When selected, it completes the expression abruptly and the assignment/print are not reached. Ten would select the unchosen default, minus one confuses selector with result, and the compile-error choice excludes a legal throwing rule. Exhaustiveness does not imply every execution completes normally.
cards.coverage_gap: Switch expression arms may terminate by throwing instead of yielding.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: the selected rule block can complete normally without yielding.
distractors: Throws IllegalStateException because no value was produced.
cards.explanation: Coverage of all selectors does not fix a block that reaches its end without yielding a value. The local declaration is not an implicit result. Java rejects this path at compile time; it neither returns seven automatically, substitutes the default zero, nor delays detection to an exception. Add an appropriate yield or throwing path.
cards.coverage_gap: Exhaustive labels and value-producing rule blocks are separate requirements.

verification.expected: switch rule completes without providing a value

distractors: Compilation fails: arrow syntax always requires exhaustiveness.
cards.explanation: Arrow syntax alone does not turn this traditional int switch statement into a switch expression or an enhanced pattern switch. With no applicable constant and no default, it does nothing, then done prints. Exhaustiveness rules are not determined solely by the arrow token. The selector does not match one, and lack of a match here does not throw.
cards.coverage_gap: Traditional arrow statement can remain nonexhaustive, unlike a switch expression.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: an arrow statement rule cannot consist of this bare numeric expression.
cards.explanation: Arrow switch statement expressions must be statement expressions, such as assignments or method calls. A bare literal is a value expression but not a statement expression. It is legal as a result in a switch expression used appropriately, not in this statement form. The code is rejected rather than discarding, printing or throwing for the numeric value.
cards.coverage_gap: Arrow switch statement and expression have different allowed expression-rule bodies.

distractors: Compilation fails: null cases require preview features.
cards.explanation: An explicit case null handles this null selector, so the expression yields missing. default alone would not handle null, but it is not the selected label here. Null handling in reference switch is available without preview for this Java target. The exception choice ignores the explicit handler, and other wrongly chooses default.
cards.coverage_gap: Explicit null case changes behavior compared with starter null selector without handler.

distractors: Compilation fails: yield cannot occur inside a loop.
cards.explanation: yield transfers the value to the enclosing switch expression and exits the rule, including the nested loop. At i=2 it supplies twenty; the later yield is not executed. Minus one treats yield as only a loop transfer, two ignores multiplication, and the nested yield is legal when its target is this enclosing switch expression.
cards.coverage_gap: Yield exits an enclosing switch expression through a nested loop.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: return cannot jump out of the enclosing switch expression.
cards.explanation: A return may not transfer control out through an enclosing switch expression. In this block, yield 7 would provide the expression result for the outer return. Neither the method value nor selector prints, and this is a compile-time transfer restriction rather than a runtime failure. Switch statement blocks allow different return usage because there is no intervening switch expression.
cards.coverage_gap: Method return cannot cross a switch-expression boundary; yield is the needed result transfer.

verification.expected: attempt to return out of a switch expression

distractors: Compilation fails: numeric switch results must have identical types.
cards.explanation: Without a target type from var, this standalone switch computes a numeric result type from both int and double alternatives, yielding double. The selected int value is converted to 4.0. Integer 4 considers only the selected branch when determining the type; 6.5 selects default incorrectly; differing numeric result types can be promoted compatibly.
cards.coverage_gap: Standalone switch numeric typing uses all result alternatives, not only the selected one.

distractors: Compilation fails: primitive values cannot be assigned to Object.
cards.explanation: This assignment gives the switch expression target type Object. Each result expression must be assignment-compatible with that target, so the selected int is boxed as Integer. Double 4.0 incorrectly applies standalone numeric promotion; 6.5 selects the wrong rule; boxing makes primitive results compatible with Object. Target context changes the typing, not which label matches.
cards.coverage_gap: Target-typed reference switch can box each result separately instead of standalone numeric promotion.

concepts.title: Reference patterns and guards
concepts.objective: Match reference types with final pattern syntax, apply guards, reason about dominance/null handling and respect pattern-variable scope.

distractors: Compilation fails: Object variables cannot hold Strings.
cards.explanation: The actual object is a String, so the pattern succeeds and binds text to it in the true branch. Object can refer to a String, and this safe type test is not an unchecked cast. not text chooses the failed-match branch. Begin with type-check plus binding before studying switch guards, dominance and more subtle flow scope.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: An instanceof type pattern checks a type and names the matched value. Which branch runs?

distractors: Compilation fails: reference type patterns require preview.
cards.explanation: The String pattern matches the actual String object and binds text to it, allowing length() without a manual cast. The expression yields four. -1 ignores a matching type, ClassCastException invents an unsafe cast, and this reference type-pattern syntax is final for the stated target. No preview primitive patterns are used.
cards.coverage_gap: Basic reference type pattern both tests type and binds the matched value.

distractors: Compilation fails: a guard cannot use its pattern variable.
cards.explanation: The String type test succeeds, binding text before its guard runs. The length test is also true, so the rule supplies long text. other ignores a satisfied guard, long confuses the original selector with the rule result, and the bound variable is available to this guard. Later variants change match/guard outcomes separately and test ordering restrictions.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: A when guard adds a boolean requirement after matching a type. Which rule applies?

distractors: Compilation fails: two String patterns always conflict.
cards.explanation: The first type pattern matches, but its guard is false. Matching continues and the next unguarded String pattern selects short. A false guard does not jump directly to default. Two same-type patterns are legal when the earlier one is guarded this way; long ignores the guard and other skips the later applicable pattern.
cards.coverage_gap: Failed guard allows a later same-type pattern rather than selecting default immediately.

cards.explanation: The guard is evaluated only after its associated pattern matches. The payload is Integer, so the String guard call is skipped and the Integer rule wins. number 1 evaluates a guard before establishing its pattern variable, text 1 ignores the type mismatch, and pattern testing does not cast an Integer to String and throw.
cards.coverage_gap: Guard side effects occur only after the associated reference type matches.

distractors: Compilation fails: null and default cannot share a label.
cards.explanation: The combined case null, default label is a legal final fallback covering both null and unmatched values. It selects fallback here. Unlike plain default, it explicitly includes null, so no exception occurs. A null value does not match the String type pattern, and this combined label is permitted without preview features for the target.
cards.coverage_gap: Combined null/default label explicitly covers both missing and unmatched reference values.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: text is not in scope after the switch expression.
cards.explanation: text is available in its matching rule, where text.length() is valid, but is not declared as a local for the following statement. The later reference is rejected. The switch does not export its pattern binding, substitute size, or give text a default null value. Use the switch result or a separately declared local when data must survive outside the rule.
cards.coverage_gap: Pattern variable is scoped to its applicable rule rather than exported from switch.

distractors: Compilation fails: guards must have primitive boolean type.
cards.explanation: A guard may have Boolean type, but evaluating it requires unboxing to decide whether it is true. The String pattern matches; approved is then unboxed and null throws. It is not treated as false or true, and the expression does not continue to default after this failure. The guard is statically legal.
cards.coverage_gap: Nullable Boolean guards can fail during matching instead of behaving as false.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: the earlier CharSequence pattern dominates String.
cards.explanation: Every non-null String also implements CharSequence, so the later String pattern can never be selected after the unguarded broad pattern. Dominance is a compile-time restriction, not a first-match choice allowed to run. Neither sequence nor string nor other prints. Put a narrower pattern first when it needs distinct handling.
cards.coverage_gap: Subtype pattern dominance prevents an unreachable narrower case.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: the unguarded String pattern dominates the go constant label.
distractors: Compilation fails: String selectors cannot use type patterns.
cards.explanation: Every selector equal to the String constant go also matches the earlier String pattern. That constant label is dominated and rejected, even though it is not another type pattern. Java does not automatically prioritize constants over source order, so neither output occurs. String selectors do permit reference type patterns; ordering is the problem. Put special constants before an unguarded pattern that covers their type.
cards.coverage_gap: Dominance also applies from an unguarded type pattern to a covered constant label.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: a constant-true guarded String case dominates the later String case.
cards.explanation: A guard that is a constant expression with value true is treated as unguarded for this dominance rule. The second String case is therefore rejected. The presence of when alone does not make every duplicate pattern legal. Compilation prevents all three output choices; a guard that can actually filter inputs is a different situation.
cards.coverage_gap: Constant-true guards are treated as unguarded for dominance.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: an unconditional pattern and default cannot both appear here.
cards.explanation: Object is unconditional for the Object selector type and already supplies the match-all coverage role. Adding default violates the switch-block rule against both kinds of match-all label. The source is rejected rather than running either output. The non-null selector would not cause a null failure; removing default addresses this compile-time problem.
cards.coverage_gap: Unconditional type pattern cannot coexist with an additional default label.

verification.expected: unconditional pattern and a default label

distractors: Compilation fails: the Object pattern cannot make the switch exhaustive.
cards.explanation: The Object pattern establishes reference-type coverage but does not act as an explicit null handler. A null selector therefore throws when there is no case null. object incorrectly treats coverage as null matching; null is not an implicit returned value; and compile-time exhaustiveness is satisfied even though this runtime null path fails.
cards.coverage_gap: Exhaustive Object type pattern still requires explicit handling for a null selector.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: a constant-false expression is not allowed as this guard.
cards.explanation: A guard that is a constant expression with value false is expressly disallowed. The compiler does not simply discard this case and choose default. Neither output nor runtime exception occurs. This restriction differs from an ordinary guard whose runtime result happens to be false, which legally allows matching to continue.
cards.coverage_gap: A constant-false guard is rejected rather than treated as a runtime filter.

concepts.title: Scope and reachable paths
concepts.objective: Respect for-variable scope and distinguish Java reachability rules for while and if.

distractors: Compilation fails: a block cannot contain local declarations.
cards.explanation: local is declared and initialized before its use in the same block, so eight prints. Zero invents a different initial value, local declarations are allowed in blocks, and reading this primitive int cannot dereference null. Later questions test where this local stops being visible and whether every path initializes it.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: A block groups work and limits local scope. What value is visible within this block?

distractors: Compilation fails: selected is only visible inside if.
Compilation fails: a branch cannot assign outer locals.
cards.explanation: selected is declared outside the branch and remains in scope after it. The true branch assigns eight to that same variable. Zero ignores assignment, branch-only visibility would describe a declaration inside the block, and ordinary mutable locals can be assigned from a nested block. Declaration location and assignment location are different.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: An outer local can be updated inside a branch. What survives after the block?

distractors: Compilation fails: main cannot use return without a value.
cards.explanation: stop is true, so the body prints and returns from void main before the final call. stopcontinue treats return as leaving only the if block, continue ignores the selected body, and a void method permits return without a value. The ordinary boolean local keeps the final statement statically reachable even though this execution does not reach it.
cards.coverage_gap: Introductory step: A return exits the current method. What happens to a later reachable statement on this path?

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: i is outside its declared scope.
distractors: It prints 2 because the loop variable survives afterward.
It prints 1 because the final body iteration used that value.
It prints 0 because the loop variable is reinitialized afterward.
cards.explanation: The for initializer variable is scoped to the loop, including its condition/update/body. It cannot be named after the loop; declare it outside when its final value is needed.

verification.code:
for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { }
System.out.print(i);

distractors: Compilation fails: the name value is duplicated inside the switch.
cards.explanation: Each explicit block has its own local scope, so the two value declarations do not conflict. Matching case two prints twenty and breaks. The compiler-error choice ignores the added blocks, ten selects the wrong case, and 1020 starts execution in case one despite the matching case two. This is a practical repair for shared-scope colon cases.
cards.coverage_gap: Separate blocks repair duplicate local declarations in colon case groups.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: colon case labels do not create separate scopes for value.
distractors: Throws IllegalStateException because value has two declarations.
cards.explanation: A case label alone does not start a new block scope. The two local declarations conflict within the switch block, regardless of which selector value executes at runtime. Neither ten nor twenty prints, and duplicate-local detection is compile-time rather than a runtime exception. Put each case body in its own braces when independent locals are needed.
cards.coverage_gap: Colon case groups share local scope unless explicit blocks separate declarations.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: the print statement after return is unreachable.
cards.explanation: An unconditional return cannot complete normally, leaving the following statement unreachable under Java rules. The method is rejected even though a human can predict a returned value. Neither one nor any late output occurs; the compiler does not silently discard this unreachable statement. A conditional return can have a reachable continuation on its other path.
cards.coverage_gap: Unconditional method return makes the following statement unreachable.

cards.explanation: Java permits an if (false) body under its special reachability rules, supporting conditional compilation patterns. The branch is not executed, and the later print runs normally.

verification.code:
if (false) { System.out.print("never"); }
System.out.print("done");

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: the while body is unreachable.
distractors: It prints done because every false branch is allowed.
It prints neverdone because the body runs before its test.
It prints nothing because the loop prevents later execution.
cards.explanation: A while with constant false has an unreachable body, which Java rejects. This differs from the special reachability rules allowing if (false) bodies and from post-tested do-while.

verification.code:
while (false) { System.out.print("never"); }
System.out.print("done");

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: the statement after the loop is unreachable.
distractors: Compilation fails: empty while bodies are forbidden.
cards.explanation: A while with constant true condition and no reachable break cannot complete normally. The following print is therefore unreachable and compilation fails. Running forever would describe the loop in isolation, but ignores the rejected following statement. done assumes an exit that is absent; empty bodies themselves are legal.
cards.coverage_gap: Constant infinite loop without break makes later code unreachable.

verification.code:
while (true) { }
System.out.print("done");

distractors: Compilation fails: loop assignments never establish definite assignment.
Compilation fails: code after while(true) is always unreachable.
cards.explanation: The reachable break allows this constant-true loop to complete normally. Every path that exits through that break has assigned limit, so the subsequent read is definitely assigned. Loop assignments can count, a reachable break changes reachability after while(true), and locals do not default to zero. The guaranteed exit matters more than the appearance of an infinite condition.
cards.coverage_gap: Reachable break from while(true) proves both exit and local assignment.

distractors: Compilation fails: a pattern variable is only in scope inside its if body.
cards.explanation: The path that fails to match returns, so any continuation past the if is known to have matched String. text is therefore in scope for the later return. Two prints for go; -1 selects the unchosen failure path, and no unsafe cast is performed. Pattern scope follows guaranteed matching paths rather than just the nearest braces.
cards.coverage_gap: Negated pattern plus abrupt guard gives a definitely matched binding after the if.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: text is not in scope where the right operand requires a failed match.
cards.explanation: The right operand of || runs when its left side is false. For this positive instanceof pattern, that path has not established a String binding, so text is unavailable there. The actual shown value does not waive static scope rules. Compilation prevents every output or exception choice. Use && for a predicate that requires a successful positive match.
cards.coverage_gap: Positive pattern variable is not available in an OR operand reached on failed match.

cards.correct_option: Compilation fails: break cannot jump through the enclosing switch expression.
cards.explanation: Even though outer names an enclosing loop, break may not cross a switch-expression boundary to reach it. The rule needs a legal result or abrupt completion permitted for expressions. Compilation rejects the transfer; it does not exit normally, substitute zero for result or throw a runtime control-flow exception. This differs from a break inside a switch statement.
cards.coverage_gap: Labeled break cannot escape through an intervening switch expression.

verification.expected: attempt to break out of a switch expression
